title: The Distant Postcards
premise: Oscar Delacroix has spent five years writing postcards to his sister Vivienne at an address that burned down, a ritual of apology he never intends to send. When a box of her undelivered letters to him surfaces behind a wardrobe in their childhood home, he learns she was alive for two years after the fire—and that she knew everything about the betrayal that destroyed them. Returning to the coastal town of Sainte-Marine where it happened, Oscar must confront the man who profited from his silence and finally choose between protecting his reputation and telling the truth. He ends by publishing Vivienne's letters verbatim, surrendering his name to her story.
about_author: Jonah Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing other people's unsent correspondence before writing fiction of his own. He lives near the sea and claims he has never mailed a letter he didn't first read aloud to an empty room.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In his cramped city apartment, Oscar writes his 1,826th postcard to Vivienne—brief, coded, almost saying it—and files it with the others. A neighbor's question about family rattles him. The beat is quiet complicity: we see a man who has made silence into a daily discipline and calls it devotion.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The executor of his aunt's estate summons him to the half-ruined house in Sainte-Marine. Moving a wardrobe, they find a tin box: forty-one letters from Vivienne, stamped but never sent, addressed to him. The last is dated eighteen months after the fire. The emotional beat is vertigo—the dead speaking back.

chapters.title: What She Knew
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, reading through the night. The letters reveal Vivienne survived the fire, hid, watched him testify falsely against her business partner Étienne Roux, and forgave him nothing. Her final line: 'Come find me before you write me again.' The beat is shame sharpening into dread—he testified to protect himself, not her.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV on the train south. Flashbacks interleave with the passing coast: the fire, the inquest, Étienne's ruined face in the dock. He rehearses confessions like postcards, all of them 'almost saying it.' The beat is a man discovering that avoidance has a geography, and he is traveling straight into its center.

chapters.title: Étienne
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He finds Étienne running a shabby boat-repair shed, unimpressed by the visit. Étienne assumes Oscar wants absolution and refuses to give it cheaply: 'You didn't come to confess. You came so I'd make it painless.' The beat is confrontation without catharsis; power still flows one way.

chapters.title: The Mayor's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Céline Marchand, a local journalist, digging into old land records. She discovers the fire cleared the waterfront lots that Mayor Aubertin sold to developers weeks later—and that Oscar's testimony was the linchpin. The beat is rising tension as an outsider begins assembling the truth Oscar buried.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Céline interviews him under a pretext; he lies smoothly, then finds one of Vivienne's unsent letters slipped into his coat pocket—someone in town has been reading the box. Paranoia blooms. The beat is the collapse of his invisibility: the art of almost saying it no longer protects anyone.

chapters.title: Aubertin's Offer
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The mayor invites him to dinner, offers money and a quiet legacy if the box disappears, revealing he's known about Vivienne's survival all along. Oscar realizes the corruption never ended—it just changed clothes. The beat is temptation rendered generous, and Oscar feeling the old machinery close around him again.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating Oscar and Céline POVs. At the town hall's centenary event, Oscar takes the microphone instead of accepting an honor, and reads Vivienne's forty-one letters aloud, ending with her final line. Aubertin's allies move to cut the power; Céline holds up her phone, recording. The beat is truth spoken past the point of recall.

chapters.title: Postcards, Sent
chapters.summary: Resolution, Oscar's POV. Months later: Aubertin indicted, Étienne restored and unreconciled but willing to share coffee, the house sold to fund a small archive of Vivienne's writings. Oscar mails every postcard he ever wrote—to the archive, not the burned address. The final beat is peace without forgiveness: he stops practicing almost saying it, because now it has been said.
